content.title: Testing Method Comparison
rows: Early concepts, complex tasks, observing nonverbal cues
Logistics, limited to local users, more expensive
Tech issues, limited observation of environment
Large sample sizes, simple tasks, quantitative data
Scale, speed, lower cost, flexible timing
No probing, limited qualitative data, less control
Quick feedback, early ideas, low budget
Limited screening, brief sessions, public setting constraints

cards.back: **Qualitative, diagnostic.** Answers WHY something happens. Best for discovering problems, understanding user behavior, and getting deep insights about specific issues.
**Quantitative, validation.** Answers WHICH version performs better. Best for comparing specific alternatives with large sample sizes to measure impact on metrics.
1. Usability testing finds problems and generates hypotheses. 2. Design solutions. 3. A/B testing validates which solution works best. 4. Usability testing explains why it worked.

cards.title: 📹 Recording & Observation
cards.details:
**Key Features Needed:**
- Screen recording
- Face/voice recording
- Note-taking synchronized to video
- Highlight/clip creation
- Easy sharing with stakeholders

cards.title: 📊 Analytics & Heatmaps
cards.details:
**What They Reveal:**
- Click heatmaps (what gets clicked)
- Scroll maps (how far users scroll)
- Session recordings (how users navigate)
- Conversion funnels (where users drop off)
cards.footer: Great for finding WHAT to test deeper

cards.title: 📋 Survey & Feedback
cards.details:
**Standardized Metrics:**
- **SUS:** 10-item questionnaire giving 0-100 score
- **NPS:** "How likely to recommend?" -100 to +100
- **SEQ:** "How easy was this task?" 1-7 scale

**Use:** Baseline measurements and track improvements.

items.definition: Percentage of users who complete a task successfully. Formula: (Successful completions / Total attempts) × 100
How long it takes users to complete a task. Compare to expert time or benchmark.
Number of errors made per task. Includes wrong clicks, incorrect inputs, navigation mistakes.
Improvement in time/success rate between first and subsequent attempts.
Post-task ratings (1-7 scale), SUS scores, NPS, or subjective satisfaction measures.

content.value:
**Benchmark Guidelines:**
- **Task Success Rate:** >78% is acceptable, >90% is good
- **Time on Task:** Should decrease with each iteration
- **SUS Score:** 68 is average, >80 is good, >90 is excellent
- **Error Rate:** Should approach zero for critical tasks

content.title: Common Objections and Responses
rows: "Fixing usability issues post-launch costs 100x more. One critical finding could save thousands in support costs." Show ROI examples.
"Even Apple tests with users. Steve Jobs famously said 'It's not the customer's job to know what they want.' We're testing if our assumptions are right."
"Post-launch fixes are expensive and damage reputation. Finding 5 issues now with 5 users prevents 5000 frustrated users later."
"That's exactly why we need to test with real users! Let's recruit exactly the users you're concerned about."

content.value: **Common Recruitment Mistakes:**
subpoints: **Testing with colleagues/friends:** They're not representative and are too familiar with your industry
**Only testing 'easy' users:** Power users miss beginner struggles
**Screening too narrowly:** Missing important edge cases or personas
**Offering wrong incentives:** Too low = poor quality, too high = professional testers

content.title: Effective Recruitment Screener
content.scenario: Recruiting for a financial planning app
content.outcome: Targeted, representative participants
content.prevention: N/A - This is a recruitment strategy
content.details:
**Screener Questions:**
1. **Age range:** 25-55 (target demographic)
2. **Employment:** Full-time employed (stability for financial planning)
3. **Financial habits:** Do you currently use any financial apps? (Mix of experienced and new users)
4. **Tech comfort:** Rate your comfort with mobile apps 1-5 (aim for distribution)
5. **Income:** $50k+ (meaningful financial decisions)
6. **Device:** Own a smartphone (technical requirement)

**Recruitment Channels:**
- LinkedIn (professional demographic)
- Reddit personal finance communities
- Local university alumni groups
- Existing user base (if any)

**Incentive:** $50 gift card for 60 minutes - professional but not excessive

content.value: **Emerging Trends:**
subpoints: **Continuous Usability Testing:** Integrated into agile sprints rather than separate phases
**AI-Assisted Analysis:** Machine learning helping identify patterns in qualitative data
**VR/AR Usability:** Testing in immersive environments with new interaction paradigms
**Voice Interface Testing:** Usability for conversational interfaces and smart assistants
**Accessibility-First Usability:** Integrating accessibility testing into all usability studies

content.value:
**The Democratization of Usability:**
Tools are making usability testing more accessible to non-specialists. While expertise still matters, more teams can now conduct basic usability testing themselves.

content.title: Your First Usability Test in 2 Weeks

steps.action: Day 1-2: Pick one critical user flow to test. Day 3-4: Write 3-5 task scenarios. Day 5: Recruit 3-5 participants (friends of friends are okay for first test).
Day 1-3: Run 1-2 tests per day. Use Zoom to record. Day 4: Analyze findings, identify top 3 issues. Day 5: Present 5-minute summary to team with video clips.
Pick the easiest-to-fix issue from your findings and implement it. Then test again to see if it helped.

content.value: **Remember These Fundamentals:**
subpoints: **Start small** - One feature, 3-5 users, simple setup
**Test early, test often** - Don't wait for "perfect" designs
**Listen, don't lead** - Your job is to learn, not to teach
**Focus on problems, not solutions** - Report what you observed, let the team design the fix
**Share the findings** - Video clips are more persuasive than reports

content.value:
Usability testing is ultimately about **empathy**—understanding your users' experiences, struggles, and needs. By regularly putting your software in front of real people and truly listening to their experiences, you move from building features to creating solutions that genuinely help people accomplish their goals.

The most usable software isn't just functional—it's intuitive, efficient, and respectful of users' time and intelligence. That's the standard to aim for, and usability testing is your guide to getting there.

cards.title: 🖼️ Beyond Functionality
cards.description: Testing the Visual Layer of Software
cards.details:
Imagine a beautiful restaurant with perfect food, but the doors are hard to open, the lights are too dim to read the menu, and the bathroom sign is confusing. The core service (food) works, but the experience is frustrating. GUI (Graphical User Interface) Testing is about checking all those visual and interactive elements that users see and touch.

While functional testing asks "Does it work?", GUI testing asks "Does it look right and behave as expected when interacted with?" It's the bridge between technical functionality and human perception. A button might technically submit a form (functional), but if it's the wrong color, misaligned, or disappears on hover (GUI), users will struggle.

content.title: GUI Bug Investigation Example
content.scenario: Report: "The sidebar looks wrong in Firefox"
content.outcome: Specific CSS compatibility issue identified
content.details:
**Observation:** Sidebar background color is white instead of light gray in Firefox.

**Investigation Steps:**
1. **Reproduce:** Open page in Firefox → confirm bug
2. **Inspect:** Firefox Dev Tools → Elements panel
3. **Compare:** Chrome vs Firefox computed styles
4. **Find:** Firefox isn't applying `background-color: #f5f5f5;`
5. **Root Cause:** CSS specificity issue. Chrome applies `.sidebar { background: #f5f5f5; }` but Firefox prioritizes conflicting rule from framework.
6. **Fix:** Increase specificity: `.app .sidebar { background: #f5f5f5 !important; }`

**Test:** Verify fix in Firefox, Chrome, Safari. No regression.

tutorials.title: Database Testing Basics
tutorials.description: Fundamental concepts of database testing for manual testers

content.title: 1. The Hidden Layer: Why Database Testing Matters

cards.title: 🧊 What Users See vs. What Actually Exists
cards.details:
Imagine an iceberg. The tip above water is your application's UI—what users see and interact with. The massive structure below water is your database—storing, organizing, and securing all the data.

**The Problem:** Most testers only test the tip (UI). They click buttons, fill forms, check outputs. But what happens underwater? When you 'delete' a user in the UI, is it really deleted from the database? Or just marked inactive? When you transfer money between accounts, does the database ensure both transactions succeed or fail together?

Database testing ensures that what happens in the UI matches what happens in the database, and that the database itself maintains data integrity, security, and performance.
cards.footer: Test what you see AND what you don't see

content.caption: Essential SQL Commands for Testers

content.title: Practical SQL for Test Validation
content.scenario: You need to verify a user registration worked correctly
content.outcome: Comprehensive data validation using SQL
content.details:
**UI Action:** Registered a new user with username 'alice123', email 'alice@test.com'

**Database Verification Steps:**
1. **Check user was created:**
   ```sql
   SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = 'alice123' OR email = 'alice@test.com';
   ```
   
2. **Verify all required fields populated:**
   ```sql
   SELECT username, email, created_at, status, verification_token 
   FROM users 
   WHERE username = 'alice123';
   ```
   
3. **Check related records (profile, settings):**
   ```sql
   SELECT * FROM user_profiles WHERE user_id = [id_from_step1];
   SELECT * FROM user_settings WHERE user_id = [id_from_step1];
   ```
   
4. **Verify no duplicate entries:**
   ```sql
   SELECT email, COUNT(*) as count 
   FROM users 
   WHERE email = 'alice@test.com' 
   GROUP BY email 
   HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
   ```

cards.title: 📊 Schema Testing
cards.details:
**What to Verify:**
- Table names and definitions match specifications
- Column names, data types, and sizes are correct
- Primary keys are defined and unique
- Foreign key relationships exist and are correct
- Indexes are present on frequently queried columns

**How to Test:**
```sql
-- Check table structure
DESCRIBE users;

-- Verify foreign key relationships
SELECT * FROM information_schema.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE 
WHERE TABLE_NAME = 'orders' AND CONSTRAINT_NAME LIKE '%fk%';

-- Check indexes
SHOW INDEX FROM users;
```

cards.title: 🔗 Relationship Testing
cards.details:
**Common Issues to Find:**
- **Orphaned Records:** Child records without parent
- **Referential Integrity Violations:** Foreign keys pointing to non-existent records
- **Circular References:** A references B, B references A

**Test Queries:**
```sql
-- Find orphaned order items (no parent order)
SELECT * FROM order_items oi
LEFT JOIN orders o ON oi.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- Find users with invalid department references
SELECT * FROM users u
LEFT JOIN departments d ON u.department_id = d.id
WHERE u.department_id IS NOT NULL AND d.id IS NULL;
```

content.title: Testing a Financial Transaction
content.scenario: User transfers $100 from Savings to Checking account
content.outcome: Comprehensive database validation
content.details:
**UI Action:** Transfer $100 from account #123 (Savings) to account #456 (Checking)

**Database Verification:**

1. **Before State (Baseline):**
   ```sql
   SELECT account_number, balance, last_updated 
   FROM accounts 
   WHERE account_number IN ('123', '456');
   ```

2. **After Transfer Verification:**
   ```sql
   -- Check balances updated correctly
   SELECT account_number, balance, 
          CASE WHEN account_number = '123' THEN 'Should be -100' 
               WHEN account_number = '456' THEN 'Should be +100' 
          END as expected_change
   FROM accounts 
   WHERE account_number IN ('123', '456');
   
   -- Verify transaction record created
   SELECT * FROM transactions 
   WHERE from_account = '123' AND to_account = '456' 
   AND amount = 100.00 
   AND status = 'completed';
   
   -- Check audit trail
   SELECT * FROM audit_log 
   WHERE entity_type = 'transaction' 
   AND action = 'transfer' 
   ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;
   ```

3. **Atomicity Check (both succeed or both fail):**
   Intentionally cause error during transfer, verify neither account balance changed.

content.title: The Works in Dev, Fails in Prod Scenario
content.scenario: Feature works perfectly in test environment with 1000 records
content.outcome: Complete failure in production with 10 million records
content.details:
**The Bug:** User search feature times out in production.

**Root Cause Investigation:**
1. **Test Environment:** 1000 users, query uses `LIKE '%search%'` - works fast
2. **Production:** 10,000,000 users, same query - takes 30+ seconds

**The Problem:**
- No index on search columns
- `LIKE` with leading wildcard can't use indexes
- Full table scan on 10M records = slow

**The Fix:**
1. Add appropriate indexes
2. Implement full-text search for better performance
3. Add pagination to limit results

**Testing Lesson:** Always test with production-scale data or understand how queries scale.

tutorials.title: Security Testing Fundamentals
tutorials.description: Basic security testing concepts and techniques

content.title: 1. The Security Mindset: Thinking Like an Adversary

cards.title: 🔒 Beyond Functional Testing
cards.details:
Imagine you've built a beautiful, functional house. Functional testing verifies: doors open, windows close, lights turn on. Security testing asks different questions:

- Can someone pick the locks?
- Are windows easy to break into?
- Can neighbors see inside?
- Are valuables left in plain sight?
- Do you give spare keys to strangers?

Security testing is the practice of evaluating software **not for what it should do**, but for **what it shouldn't allow to happen**. It's about finding vulnerabilities before malicious actors do. While functional testing asks 'Does it work?', security testing asks 'Can it be broken or abused?'

content.title: Security Testing vs. Functional Testing
rows: Login with SQL injection, brute force

content.title: 2. The OWASP Top 10: Every Tester's Essential Guide

content.value: The **Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP)** is a nonprofit foundation that works to improve software security. Their **OWASP Top 10** is the industry-standard awareness document representing the most critical security risks to web applications.

items.definition: Based on real-world data from thousands of organizations and hundreds of thousands of applications
Prioritizes based on exploitability, detectability, and impact
Provides specific prevention techniques and testing guidance
Updated every 3-4 years to reflect changing threat landscape

content.title: OWASP Top 10 Web Application Security Risks
rows: Users can act outside intended permissions
Try accessing admin pages as regular user
Check if passwords/credit cards are encrypted
Untrusted data sent to interpreter as part of command
Enter SQL code in form fields: ' OR '1'='1
Can you bypass business logic flows?
Default configurations, unnecessary features, error messages
Check for default passwords, verbose errors
Check library versions against known vulnerabilities
Test weak passwords, no lockout, credential stuffing
Check for unsigned updates, insecure CI/CD
Insufficient logging and monitoring (formerly 'Insufficient Logging & Monitoring')
Do attacks leave traces? Are logs reviewed?
Making requests from server to internal resources
Can you make server fetch internal files/APIs?

cards.title: 🔍 Information Gathering
cards.details:
**Techniques:**
- **View Source:** Check for comments, hidden fields, API keys
- **Robots.txt:** See what search engines shouldn't index
- **Directory Brute Force:** Try common directories (/admin, /backup, /test)
- **Error Messages:** Trigger errors to learn about technology stack

**Tools:**
- Browser Developer Tools
- Curl or Postman for API exploration
- Built-in browser 'View Source'

**Ethical Note:** Only test systems you own or have explicit permission to test.

cards.title: 💉 Input Validation Testing
cards.details:
**Test Inputs:**
- **SQL Injection:** `' OR '1'='1`, `'; DROP TABLE users;--`
- **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting):** `<script>alert('XSS')</script>`
- **Command Injection:** `; ls -la`, `| dir`, `&& whoami`
- **Path Traversal:** `../../../etc/passwd`

**Where to Test:**
- All form fields
- URL parameters
- HTTP headers
- File uploads
- API endpoints

cards.title: 🔑 Authentication Testing
cards.details:
**Test Scenarios:**
- Weak password policy (no complexity requirements)
- No account lockout after failed attempts
- Password visible in browser (type='text')
- Remember me functionality with weak encryption
- Password reset vulnerabilities
- Session management issues

**Common Issues:**
- Session IDs in URLs
- No session timeout
- Concurrent logins allowed
- Logout doesn't invalidate session
cards.footer: The front door must be strong

content.title: Testing a Login Form for Security

steps.action: Check error messages: Enter wrong password. Does it say 'Invalid password' (good) or 'User not found' (bad - reveals valid users)?
Username: `admin'--` Password: anything. Does it log in? Try: `' OR '1'='1`
Attempt 10 wrong passwords in a row. Does account lock? Is there delay? CAPTCHA?
Try weak passwords: 'password', '123456', 'admin'. Are they accepted?
Login, copy session cookie, logout, try to reuse cookie. Does it work?
Check if login is over HTTPS (not HTTP). Are credentials encrypted in transit?

content.title: Real SQL Injection Test
content.scenario: Testing a search feature on an e-commerce site
content.outcome: Discovered critical vulnerability
content.details:
**Vulnerable Search:** `https://example.com/search?q=laptop`

**Test 1: Basic Injection**
`https://example.com/search?q=laptop' OR '1'='1`
**Result:** Returns ALL products instead of just laptops

**Test 2: Database Exploration**
`https://example.com/search?q=laptop' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users--`
**Result:** Shows user credentials alongside products

**Test 3: More Dangerous**
`https://example.com/search?q=laptop'; DROP TABLE products;--`
**WARNING:** Never test destructive queries on production!

**The Fix:**
```python
# Vulnerable
query = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '" + user_input + "'"

# Secure (parameterized)
query = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = %s"
cursor.execute(query, (user_input,))
```

steps.action: Use virtual machines or containers isolated from production. Never test on live systems.

content.value: Access control ensures users can only access what they're authorized to. Broken access control is consistently the #1 risk in OWASP Top 10.

items.definition: Accessing another user's data at the same privilege level. Test: User A accesses User B's data by changing IDs in URLs/parameters.
Accessing functions/data of a higher privilege level. Test: Regular user accesses admin functions.
Accessing objects directly by modifying references. Test: `/user/123/profile` → `/user/124/profile`.
Accessing hidden URLs/directories. Test: `/admin`, `/backup`, `/config`.

content.title: Testing for IDOR Vulnerability
content.scenario: E-commerce site with order viewing feature
content.outcome: Discovered users can view each other's orders
content.prevention: Authorization checks on all object accesses
content.details:
**Normal Flow:**
User logs in → Clicks 'My Orders' → Sees `GET /orders/123` (their order)

**Vulnerability Test:**
1. User A logs in, finds their order ID: `123`
2. User A changes URL to: `GET /orders/124`
3. **Result:** Sees User B's order details

**The Bug:**
Backend code:
```python
# Vulnerable
order = Order.objects.get(id=order_id)
return render('order_details.html', {'order': order})

# Secure
order = Order.objects.get(id=order_id, user=request.user)
if not order:
    return HttpResponseForbidden()
```

**Testing Pattern:**
Always test if you can access other users' data by changing IDs in URLs, parameters, or API requests.

cards.title: 📝 Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
cards.details:
**How it works:**
- Scans source code without executing it
- Looks for patterns indicating vulnerabilities
- Can be integrated into IDEs and CI/CD

**Pros:**
- Finds issues early
- Can scan 100% of code
- Low false positives for certain issues

**Cons:**
- Can't find runtime issues
- May have false positives
- Requires source code access

**Tools:** SonarQube, Checkmarx, Fortify

cards.title: ⚡ Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
cards.details:
**How it works:**
- Tests application from the outside (black-box)
- Sends malicious inputs, analyzes responses
- Doesn't need source code

**Pros:**
- Finds runtime vulnerabilities
- Tests actual deployment configuration
- Can find configuration issues

**Cons:**
- Can't test 100% of code paths
- Later in development cycle
- May miss business logic flaws

**Tools:** OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Acunetix

cards.title: 🧪 Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)
cards.details:
**How it works:**
- Instrumentation agents in running application
- Monitors execution for vulnerabilities
- Combines code analysis with runtime data

**Pros:**
- More accurate than SAST or DAST alone
- Lower false positive rate
- Provides runtime context

**Cons:**
- Requires application instrumentation
- Performance overhead
- More complex setup

**Tools:** Contrast Security, Seeker, Synopsys IAST

content.value: A good security finding has three parts: what's wrong, why it matters, and how to fix it.

content.caption: Security Finding Report Template
content.code:
# Security Finding: SQL Injection in Search Feature

## Basic Information
- **ID:** SEC-2024-001
- **Severity:** Critical
- **Component:** Product Search API
- **Location:** `GET /api/search?q=<query>`
- **Discovered:** 2024-03-15
- **Tester:** Jane Doe

## Description
The search endpoint is vulnerable to SQL injection attacks, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands on the database.

## Proof of Concept
### Steps to Reproduce:
1. Navigate to: `https://example.com/search?q=laptop`
2. Change query to: `https://example.com/search?q=laptop' OR '1'='1`
3. Observe: Returns all products instead of just laptops

### Additional Tests:
- `q=laptop' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users--` (Extracts credentials)
- `q=laptop'; SELECT SLEEP(5)--` (Time-based blind injection)

## Impact Assessment
### Technical Impact:
- Full database compromise
- Data theft (user credentials, PII, financial data)
- Data corruption or deletion
- Possible server compromise via command execution

### Business Impact:
- **Financial:** Potential fines (GDPR, PCI DSS), breach costs
- **Reputational:** Loss of customer trust, brand damage
- **Operational:** Service disruption, recovery costs

## Root Cause
The application concatenates user input directly into SQL queries without parameterization:

```python
# Vulnerable code (search.py, line 42)
query = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%" + user_input + "%'"
cursor.execute(query)
```

## Remediation
### Immediate Action:
1. Disable the search feature temporarily
2. Monitor logs for exploitation attempts

### Code Fix:
Use parameterized queries:
```python
# Secure code
query = "SELECT * FROM products WHERE name LIKE %s"
search_term = "%" + user_input + "%"
cursor.execute(query, (search_term,))
```

### Additional Recommendations:
1. Implement web application firewall (WAF)
2. Add input validation (allowlist acceptable characters)
3. Implement least privilege database accounts
4. Conduct security training for developers

## References
- OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet
- CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements
- PCI DSS Requirement 6.5.1

## Status
- [ ] Open
- [ ] In Progress
- [ ] Fixed
- [ ] Retested
- [ ] Closed

content.value:
**The DREAD Model for Risk Assessment:**
- **Damage Potential:** How bad would an attack be?
- **Reproducibility:** How easy is it to reproduce the attack?
- **Exploitability:** How easy is it to launch an attack?
- **Affected Users:** How many users would be affected?
- **Discoverability:** How easy is it to find the vulnerability?

**Score each 1-3, sum for total risk score (3-15).**

content.title: 8. Ethics, Laws, and Your Security Journey

content.value: Security testing walks a fine line between protection and intrusion. Understanding ethics and laws is non-negotiable.

items.definition: Never test systems you don't own or have explicit written permission to test.
Stay within the agreed testing scope. Don't test systems/features not included in authorization.
Avoid destructive testing unless specifically authorized. Use test accounts, not production data.
Protect all findings. Only share with authorized parties. Don't disclose vulnerabilities publicly without permission.
Report findings objectively, without exaggeration. Help fix issues, don't just point them out.

content.title: Understanding Performance Testing
content.explanation: Performance testing is a non-functional testing practice that evaluates how a system behaves under various conditions, focusing on responsiveness, stability, scalability, and resource usage. Unlike functional testing that verifies 'what' the system does, performance testing evaluates 'how well' it does it under specific loads. This practice helps identify bottlenecks, establish baselines, and ensure the application meets performance requirements before production deployment. Effective performance testing prevents costly post-release failures and ensures positive user experiences even under peak loads.

items: Load Testing: Measuring system behavior under expected user load
Stress Testing: Determining system limits and breaking points
Endurance Testing: Evaluating performance over extended periods
Spike Testing: Assessing system response to sudden load increases
Scalability Testing: Measuring ability to scale with increased resources

content.value: Performance testing types serve different strategic purposes throughout the software development lifecycle. Load testing validates everyday performance, stress testing uncovers failure modes, endurance testing identifies memory leaks, spike testing prepares for marketing events, and scalability testing informs infrastructure planning. Each type requires different test designs, execution strategies, and success criteria.

content.value: Performance requirements should be defined using SMART criteria: Specific (clearly defined metrics), Measurable (quantifiable values), Achievable (technically feasible), Relevant (business impact), and Time-bound (response time targets). Common requirements include response time percentiles (95th/99th percentile), throughput (transactions per second), concurrent users, and resource utilization limits.

Performance test planning involves defining test objectives, identifying critical user journeys, estimating load patterns, selecting appropriate tools, and establishing success criteria. A comprehensive test plan should consider business cycles, geographic distribution, and realistic user behavior patterns.

content.title: Understanding Digital Accessibility
content.explanation: Accessibility testing ensures that digital products can be used by people with diverse abilities and disabilities, including visual, auditory, motor, cognitive, and neurological impairments. Unlike general usability testing, accessibility testing specifically evaluates compliance with established standards (primarily WCAG) and compatibility with assistive technologies. This practice is both a legal requirement in many jurisdictions and a business imperative that expands market reach, improves SEO, and enhances overall user experience. Effective accessibility testing requires understanding both technical standards and human experiences of disability.

content.value: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) provide the international standard for digital accessibility, organized around four principles: Perceivable (information must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive), Operable (interface components must be operable), Understandable (information and operation must be understandable), and Robust (content must be robust enough to be interpreted reliably by various user agents). Each principle has guidelines, success criteria (with A, AA, AAA conformance levels), and sufficient/ advisory techniques for implementation.

content.value: Automated accessibility testing tools can identify approximately 30-40% of WCAG issues but must be supplemented with manual testing. Tools range from browser extensions for quick checks to enterprise scanners for comprehensive audits. Integration into CI/CD pipelines enables early detection of accessibility regressions.

content.title: Comprehensive Accessibility Testing Methodology

A successful accessibility program balances compliance checking with usability evaluation, recognizing that technically accessible interfaces may still present usability barriers. Testing should consider diverse user scenarios, varying technology configurations, and real-world usage contexts.

content.title: Understanding Browser Compatibility
content.explanation: Browser compatibility testing ensures web applications function consistently across different browsers, versions, and operating systems. Each browser uses different rendering engines (Blink, Gecko, WebKit) and JavaScript engines that interpret code differently, leading to variations in layout, functionality, and performance. Effective compatibility testing requires understanding these engine differences, market share analysis, and strategic prioritization based on target audience. The goal is to provide a consistent user experience while balancing testing efforts against business requirements and technical constraints.

items: Browser rendering engines and JavaScript engine differences

content.value: Different browser engines interpret HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in unique ways, causing compatibility challenges. Blink (Chrome, Edge, Opera) is Chromium-based with rapid updates. Gecko (Firefox) emphasizes standards compliance and privacy. WebKit (Safari) dominates Apple ecosystems with conservative feature adoption. Legacy engines like Trident (IE) require special handling. Understanding these differences helps predict and resolve compatibility issues.

content.title: Understanding Responsive Design Testing
content.explanation: Responsive design testing validates that web applications adapt correctly to different screen sizes, resolutions, orientations, and devices. Unlike traditional testing that focuses on fixed layouts, responsive testing examines how design elements reflow, resize, and reorganize across breakpoints. This involves testing visual consistency, functional behavior, and user interactions across the entire spectrum of viewport sizes. Effective responsive testing requires understanding CSS media queries, fluid grids, flexible images, and mobile-first or adaptive design approaches.

items: Fluid grid and flexible image testing

content.value: Breakpoints are specific screen widths where layout changes occur through CSS media queries. Testing must verify that transitions between breakpoints are smooth, content remains accessible, and no horizontal scrollbars appear. Common breakpoints include mobile (320px-480px), tablet (481px-768px), small desktop (769px-1024px), and large desktop (1025px+). However, modern responsive design increasingly uses content-based breakpoints rather than device-based ones.

content.title: Understanding Cookie Testing Fundamentals
content.explanation: Cookie testing validates that web applications properly create, manage, and utilize cookies for session management, personalization, tracking, and authentication purposes. Cookies are small text files stored by browsers that contain data sent between web servers and clients. Effective cookie testing requires understanding different cookie types (session, persistent, secure, HttpOnly), their attributes (domain, path, expiration), and their impact on user experience, security, and privacy. Testing must encompass functionality validation, security assessment, compliance verification, and performance evaluation across various browsers and devices.

items: Storage limits and performance impact assessment

content.value: Cookie functionality testing ensures cookies are created, read, updated, and deleted correctly according to application requirements. This involves testing different cookie types: session cookies (temporary, browser-session only), persistent cookies (with expiration dates), secure cookies (HTTPS only), and HttpOnly cookies (inaccessible to JavaScript). Each cookie type serves specific purposes and has different testing requirements for creation timing, storage duration, accessibility, and deletion behavior.

content.title: Understanding Session Testing
content.explanation: Session testing validates that web applications properly manage user sessions from creation through destruction, ensuring secure and seamless user experiences. Sessions represent authenticated user interactions with the application, typically managed through cookies, tokens, or server-side storage. Effective session testing requires understanding session lifecycle management, timeout handling, security mechanisms, and state persistence across various interruption scenarios. This testing is critical for both security (preventing session hijacking, fixation, and replay attacks) and usability (maintaining user state, preventing data loss, and enabling smooth workflows).

content.value: Session lifecycle testing validates the complete journey of a user session from initial authentication to final termination. This includes testing session creation on login, maintenance during user activity, timeout handling during inactivity, and proper destruction on logout or expiration. Each phase has specific testing requirements and common failure points that must be systematically validated to ensure both security and user experience.

content.title: Core Security Vulnerabilities and Testing Approaches
Understanding Web Security Testing Fundamentals
content.explanation: Web security testing systematically evaluates web applications for vulnerabilities that could be exploited by malicious actors. This practice combines automated scanning with manual testing techniques to identify security weaknesses in authentication, authorization, input validation, session management, and data protection. Effective security testing follows the OWASP Top 10 framework as a baseline while adapting to specific application architectures and business contexts. The goal is to discover vulnerabilities before attackers do, allowing for remediation that protects user data, maintains application integrity, and ensures regulatory compliance.

content.title: Practical Security Assessment Methodologies
content.explanation: Practical web security testing combines automated vulnerability scanning with manual penetration testing techniques to provide comprehensive coverage. This involves using specialized security tools for discovery and initial assessment, followed by manual exploitation and validation of identified vulnerabilities. Effective security testing follows a structured methodology: reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, exploitation, post-exploitation analysis, and reporting. Understanding both automated tool capabilities and manual testing techniques enables testers to identify complex vulnerabilities that tools might miss while efficiently covering common issues.

content.title: Understanding File Upload Testing
content.explanation: File upload testing validates that web applications correctly accept, process, store, and manage user-uploaded files while maintaining security, performance, and usability. This testing encompasses file type validation, size restrictions, naming conventions, storage management, and security controls. Effective file upload testing requires understanding both client-side validation (user interface feedback) and server-side validation (security and processing). The testing must address common vulnerabilities like malicious file uploads, path traversal attacks, and denial of service while ensuring smooth user experiences for legitimate file transfers.

content.value:
import stripe
import pytest
from datetime import datetime

class TestPaymentWorkflow:
    
    def setup_method(self):
        self.stripe = stripe.Stripe(api_key='test_key')
        self.order_id = f"ORD-{datetime.now().strftime('%Y%m%d%H%M%S')}"
    
    def test_successful_payment_flow(self):
        """Test complete payment authorization and capture"""
        # 1. Create payment intent
        intent = self.stripe.PaymentIntent.create(
            amount=10000,
            currency='usd',
            payment_method_types=['card'],
            capture_method='manual',  # Authorize now, capture later
            metadata={'order_id': self.order_id}
        )
        
        # 2. Authorize payment
        authorized = self.stripe.PaymentIntent.confirm(
            intent.id,
            payment_method='pm_card_visa'
        )
        assert authorized.status == 'requires_capture'
        
        # 3. Capture payment
        captured = self.stripe.PaymentIntent.capture(intent.id)
        assert captured.status == 'succeeded'
        
        # 4. Verify order status update
        order = get_order(self.order_id)
        assert order.status == 'paid'
        assert order.payment_id == intent.id
    
    def test_partial_refund(self):
        """Test partial refund scenario"""
        # Create and capture payment
        intent = self.create_and_capture_payment(5000)
        
        # Process partial refund
        refund = self.stripe.Refund.create(
            payment_intent=intent.id,
            amount=2000  # Refund $20 of $50
        )
        
        assert refund.status == 'succeeded'
        assert refund.amount == 2000
        
        # Verify order updated
        order = get_order(self.order_id)
        assert order.refunded_amount == 2000
        assert order.status == 'partially_refunded'

#!/bin/bash

# Test for PCI DSS compliance

echo "Running PCI DSS Security Tests..."

# 1. Check TLS configuration
openssl s_client -connect payments.example.com:443 \
  -tls1_2 <<< "Q" | grep "TLSv1.2"

# 2. Test for sensitive data exposure
grep -r "PAN\|Primary Account Number" /var/log/ \
  || echo "No PAN found in logs - PASS"

# 3. Verify no card data in forms
curl -s https://checkout.example.com | \
  grep -i "card.*number\|cvv\|expiry" \
  && echo "WARNING: Card field names found" \
  || echo "No card field names - PASS"

# 4. Check security headers
curl -I https://payments.example.com | \
  grep -i "strict-transport-security\|content-security-policy"

# 5. Test vulnerability scanning
# Using OWASP ZAP for automated scanning
zap-cli quick-scan --self-contained \
  --start-options '-config api.disablekey=true' \
  https://payments.example.com/checkout

# 6. Verify no sensitive data in source
find . -name "*.js" -type f -exec grep -l "4242" {} \; \
  && echo "WARNING: Test card numbers in source" \
  || echo "No test cards in source - PASS"

      expect(result.amount).to eq(10000)

      # Mock exchange rate: 1 EUR = 1.10 USD
      allow(ExchangeRate).to receive(:convert)
        .with(10000, 'EUR', 'USD')
        .and_return(11000)
      
      result = payment_gateway.charge(
        amount: 10000,  # €100.00
        currency: 'EUR',
        card: test_card(:mastercard)
      )
      
      expect(result).to be_success
      expect(result.base_amount).to eq(10000)
      expect(result.converted_amount).to eq(11000)
    end
    
    it 'handles currency-specific formatting' do
      # Japanese Yen (no decimal places)
      result = payment_gateway.charge(
        amount: 1000,  # ¥1000
        currency: 'JPY',
        card: test_card(:visa)
      )
      
      expect(result.formatted_amount).to eq('¥1,000')
    end
  end
  
  describe 'regional payment methods' do
    it 'processes iDEAL payments for Netherlands' do
      result = payment_gateway.process_ideal(
        amount: 5000,
        issuer: 'ABNANL2A',
        return_url: 'https://example.com/return'
      )
      
      expect(result).to be_redirect
      expect(result.redirect_url).to include('ideal')
    end
    
    it 'processes SEPA direct debit for EU' do
      result = payment_gateway.process_sepa(
        amount: 7500,
        iban: 'DE89370400440532013000',
        mandate: sepa_mandate
      )
      
      expect(result).to be_success
      expect(result.payment_method).to eq('sepa_debit')
    end
    
    it 'handles Brazil's installment payments' do
      # Brazilian customers often pay in installments
      result = payment_gateway.process_brazil_card(
        amount: 100000,  # R$1000.00
        card: test_card(:elo),
        installments: 10
      )
      
      expect(result.installments).to eq(10)
      expect(result.installment_amount).to eq(10000)  # R$100.00 per installment
    end
  end
  
  describe 'tax and compliance' do
    it 'calculates VAT for EU customers' do
      order = Order.new(
        amount: 10000,
        customer_country: 'DE',  # Germany
        customer_vat_id: 'DE123456789'
      )
      
      tax_calculator = TaxCalculator.new
      tax_result = tax_calculator.calculate_for_order(order)
      
      expect(tax_result.vat_rate).to eq(0.19)  # 19% German VAT
      expect(tax_result.vat_amount).to eq(1900)
      expect(tax_result.total_amount).to eq(11900)
    end
    
    it 'validates Strong Customer Authentication for EU' do
      # Test SCA exemptions
      result = payment_gateway.process_with_sca(
        amount: 2999,  # Below €30 - low-value exemption
        currency: 'EUR',
        card: test_card(:visa),
        exemption: 'low_value'

        amount: 10000,  # €100 - requires SCA
        currency: 'EUR',
        card: test_card(:visa)
      )

content.title: Understanding Manual API Testing
content.explanation: Manual API testing involves systematically validating API endpoints without automated scripts, focusing on functionality, reliability, performance, and security. Unlike automated testing, manual testing allows testers to explore edge cases, validate business logic, and assess user experience through direct interaction with APIs. This approach is essential for initial API validation, exploratory testing, and scenarios where automation may be impractical or premature. Effective manual API testing requires understanding HTTP methods, status codes, request/response formats, and authentication mechanisms.

content.value: HTTP methods form the foundation of API interactions. GET retrieves data, POST creates resources, PUT updates entire resources, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE removes resources. Understanding proper method usage is critical for testing API behavior correctly.

content.caption: Basic cURL Commands for API Testing
content.value:
# GET request - Retrieve user data
curl -X GET https://api.example.com/users/123 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token123"

# POST request - Create new user
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token123" \
  -d '{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "email": "john@example.com",
    "role": "user"
  }'

# PUT request - Update entire user
curl -X PUT https://api.example.com/users/123 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token123" \
  -d '{
    "name": "John Updated",
    "email": "john.updated@example.com",
    "role": "admin"
  }'

# PATCH request - Partial update
curl -X PATCH https://api.example.com/users/123 \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token123" \
  -d '{"email": "newemail@example.com"}'

# DELETE request - Remove user
curl -X DELETE https://api.example.com/users/123 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer token123"

# View response headers only
curl -I https://api.example.com/users/123

# Save response to file
curl -o response.json https://api.example.com/users

HTTP status codes indicate API response outcomes. 2xx codes indicate success, 3xx indicate redirection, 4xx indicate client errors, and 5xx indicate server errors. Manual testers must validate that APIs return appropriate status codes for different scenarios.

#!/bin/bash

# Test API key authentication
# Valid API key
curl -X GET https://api.example.com/data \
  -H "X-API-Key: valid-api-key-123"

# Missing API key

  -H "Content-Type: application/json"

# Invalid API key

  -H "X-API-Key: invalid-key"

  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."

#!/bin/bash

# Test numeric boundary values for age field
# Valid minimum age (18)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Test", "age": 18}'

# Just below minimum (17)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Test", "age": 17}'

# Valid maximum age (120)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Test", "age": 120}'

# Just above maximum (121)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Test", "age": 121}'

# Test string length boundaries
# Minimum length string (1 character)
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "A", "email": "a@b.com"}'

# Maximum length string (255 characters)
long_name=$(printf '%255s' | tr ' ' 'A')
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"name\": \"$long_name\", \"email\": \"test@example.com\"}"

# Exceeds maximum length (256 characters)
too_long_name=$(printf '%256s' | tr ' ' 'A')
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"name\": \"$too_long_name\", \"email\": \"test@example.com\"}"

# Test empty values
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "", "email": "test@example.com"}'

# Test null values
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": null, "email": "test@example.com"}'

# Test missing required fields
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email": "test@example.com"}'  # Missing name

# Test wrong data types
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": 123, "email": "test@example.com"}'  # Name should be string

# Test malformed JSON
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/users \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Test" "email": "test@example.com"}'  # Missing comma

# Test SQL injection attempts
curl -X GET "https://api.example.com/users?name=' OR '1'='1"

# Test XSS payloads
curl -X POST https://api.example.com/comments \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"comment": "<script>alert(\"xss\")</script>"}'

content.value:
import requests
import json
from datetime import datetime

class APISecurityTester:
    def __init__(self, base_url, auth_token):
        self.base_url = base_url
        self.auth_token = auth_token
        self.headers = {
            'Authorization': f'Bearer {auth_token}',
            'Content-Type': 'application/json'
        }
    
    def test_idor(self, endpoint_pattern, resource_ids):
        """Test for Insecure Direct Object Reference vulnerabilities"""
        print("\n=== Testing IDOR Vulnerabilities ===")
        
        for resource_id in resource_ids:
            url = f"{self.base_url}{endpoint_pattern.format(id=resource_id)}"
            response = requests.get(url, headers=self.headers)
            
            print(f"Testing {url}")
            print(f"Status: {response.status_code}")
            
            if response.status_code == 200:
                print("WARNING: Possible IDOR vulnerability - accessed resource", resource_id)
                try:
                    data = response.json()
                    print(f"Data returned: {json.dumps(data, indent=2)[:200]}...")
                except:
                    print(f"Response: {response.text[:200]}...")
            print("-" * 50)
    
    def test_sql_injection(self, endpoint, params):
        """Test for SQL injection vulnerabilities"""
        print("\n=== Testing SQL Injection ===")
        
        sql_payloads = [
            "' OR '1'='1",
            "'; DROP TABLE users; --",
            "' UNION SELECT NULL, username, password FROM users --",
            "1' AND SLEEP(5) --"
        ]
        
        for payload in sql_payloads:
            test_params = params.copy()
            for key in test_params:
                if isinstance(test_params[key], str):
                    test_params[key] = payload
            
            start_time = datetime.now()
            response = requests.get(endpoint, params=test_params, headers=self.headers)
            elapsed = (datetime.now() - start_time).total_seconds()
            
            print(f"Payload: {payload}")
            print(f"Status: {response.status_code}, Time: {elapsed:.2f}s")
            
            # Check for time-based SQL injection
            if elapsed > 4:
                print("WARNING: Possible time-based SQL injection detected")
            
            # Check for error messages revealing SQL structure
            if "sql" in response.text.lower() or "syntax" in response.text.lower():
                print("WARNING: SQL error message exposed")
    
    def test_auth_bypass(self, endpoints):
        """Test authentication bypass techniques"""
        print("\n=== Testing Authentication Bypass ===")
        
        # Test without authentication
        no_auth_headers = {'Content-Type': 'application/json'}
        
        for endpoint in endpoints:
            response = requests.get(f"{self.base_url}{endpoint}", headers=no_auth_headers)
            print(f"{endpoint} without auth: {response.status_code}")
            
            if response.status_code == 200:
                print("CRITICAL: Authentication bypass possible!")
            
        # Test with modified JWT (if using JWT)
        if 'Bearer' in self.headers['Authorization']:
            token = self.headers['Authorization'].replace('Bearer ', '')
            parts = token.split('.')
            
            if len(parts) == 3:
                # Try tampering with payload
                import base64
                try:
                    payload = json.loads(base64.b64decode(parts[1] + '==').decode('utf-8'))
                    payload['role'] = 'admin'  # Try to escalate privileges
                    
                    # Re-encode (without signature validation for test)
                    tampered_token = parts[0] + '.' + \
                        base64.b64encode(json.dumps(payload).encode()).decode().rstrip('=') + '.' + parts[2]
                    
                    tampered_headers = {'Authorization': f'Bearer {tampered_token}'}
                    response = requests.get(f"{self.base_url}/admin", headers=tampered_headers)
                    
                    print(f"\nJWT tampering test: {response.status_code}")
                    if response.status_code == 200:
                        print("CRITICAL: JWT signature not validated!")
                except:
                    print("JWT tampering test skipped (token format issue)")
    
    def test_rate_limiting(self, endpoint):
        """Test rate limiting implementation"""
        print("\n=== Testing Rate Limiting ===")
        
        responses = []
        for i in range(15):  # Send 15 rapid requests
            response = requests.get(f"{self.base_url}{endpoint}", headers=self.headers)
            responses.append({
                'request': i+1,
                'status': response.status_code,
                'headers': dict(response.headers)
            })
            
        # Analyze responses
        rate_limited = [r for r in responses if r['status'] == 429]
        print(f"Requests sent: {len(responses)}")
        print(f"Rate limited responses: {len(rate_limited)}")
        
        if rate_limited:
            print(f"First rate limit at request #{rate_limited[0]['request']}")
            print("Rate limit headers:", rate_limited[0]['headers'].get('X-RateLimit-Limit', 'Not found'))
        else:
            print("WARNING: No rate limiting detected")

# Example usage
if __name__ == "__main__":
    tester = APISecurityTester(
        base_url="https://api.example.com",
        auth_token="your-test-token-here"
    )
    
    # Run security tests
    tester.test_idor("/users/{id}", [123, 456, 789])
    tester.test_sql_injection("/users/search", {"q": "test"})
    tester.test_auth_bypass(["/users/me", "/admin/dashboard"])
    tester.test_rate_limiting("/api/data")

content.title: Postman for REST API Testing
content.explanation: Postman is a comprehensive API development and testing platform that enables manual and automated testing of RESTful APIs. It provides an intuitive interface for building requests, organizing tests into collections, automating test execution, and generating documentation. Postman's testing capabilities include JavaScript-based test scripts, environment variables, pre-request scripts, and response validation. This tool is essential for API testers to efficiently validate API functionality, security, and performance across different development stages.

items: Postman interface and request building fundamentals

content.value: Understanding Postman's interface is crucial for efficient API testing. The workspace consists of the request builder (URL, method, headers, body), response viewer (status, body, headers, cookies), and tabs for tests, pre-request scripts, and settings. Collections organize related requests, while environments manage variables for different testing stages (development, staging, production).

content.caption: Basic Postman Request Structure

content.value: Collections provide organization for API tests. A well-structured collection uses folders for logical grouping (by resource, by functionality), includes request descriptions, and uses naming conventions. Collection runners enable batch execution of requests with data-driven testing capabilities.

content.value: Environment and variable management in Postman enables testing across different configurations. Environments store variable sets for different stages (development, testing, production), while collection variables are shared across all requests in a collection. Dynamic variables can be set during request execution.

content.value: Request authentication in Postman supports various methods including API keys, Bearer tokens, Basic auth, OAuth 2.0, and AWS Signature. Postman's Authorization tab simplifies token management and automatic token renewal for OAuth flows.

content.title: Postman Automation and CI/CD Integration
content.explanation: Postman's advanced testing capabilities enable automation through the built-in test sandbox, collection runners, and Newman CLI tool. Test automation in Postman uses JavaScript for assertions, response validation, and workflow orchestration. Integration with CI/CD pipelines through Newman allows automated API testing as part of development workflows. Advanced features include data-driven testing, mock servers, monitoring, and API documentation generation.

content.value: Postman test scripting uses the pm (Postman sandbox) API for assertions, environment manipulation, and request control. Tests can validate status codes, response times, JSON schemas, and business logic. The test sandbox provides libraries like Chai for assertions and Lodash for utilities.

content.value: Newman is Postman's command-line collection runner that enables API testing in CI/CD pipelines. It executes collections, generates reports, and integrates with testing frameworks. Newman supports various reporters (HTML, JSON, JUnit) for test result visualization.

#!/bin/bash

# ===== BASIC NEWMAN COMMANDS =====

# Run a collection

# Run with environment

  -e "Development Environment.postman_environment.json"

# Run with data file
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -d "test-data.json" \
  -e "Testing Environment.postman_environment.json"

# Run with globals
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -g "Global Variables.postman_environment.json"

# ===== REPORTING OPTIONS =====

# HTML report
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -r html,cli \
  --reporter-html-export "test-report.html"

# JUnit report for CI/CD integration
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -r junit,cli \
  --reporter-junit-export "junit-report.xml"

# JSON report for programmatic processing
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -r json,cli \
  --reporter-json-export "newman-report.json"

# Multiple reporters
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -r htmlextra,cli,junit \
  --reporter-htmlextra-export "html-report.html" \
  --reporter-junit-export "junit-report.xml"

# ===== ADVANCED OPTIONS =====

# Set iteration count
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  -n 5  # Run 5 iterations

# Delay between requests
newman run "User API Tests.postman_collection.json" \
  --delay-request 1000  # 1 second delay

# Timeout settings

  --timeout-request 5000 \  # Request timeout (5 seconds)
  --timeout-script 5000     # Script timeout (5 seconds)

Postman Mock Servers create simulated API endpoints for testing without backend dependencies. Monitors schedule automated collection runs and alert on failures. Documentation generation creates interactive API docs from collections. These features support comprehensive API testing workflows from development to production monitoring.

#!/bin/bash

# Create mock server from collection

postman mock create \
  --collection "User API Tests" \
  --name "User API Mock Server" \
  --environment "Mock Environment" \
  --delay 200 \
  --port 3000

# Mock server response examples in collection

#           "body": "{\"error\":\"Unauthorized\"}"
#         }
#       ]
#     }
#   ]
# }

# ===== MONITOR SETUP =====

# Create monitor for collection
postman monitor create \
  --collection "User API Tests" \
  --name "Production API Monitor" \
  --environment "Production Environment" \
  --interval "30" \  # Run every 30 minutes
  --delay 1000 \
  --timeout 5000

# Monitor options:
# --interval: 5, 10, 15, 30, 60, 180, 360, 720, 1440 (minutes)
# --delay: Delay between requests in monitor run
# --timeout: Request timeout

# Run monitor manually
postman monitor run \
  --monitor "Production API Monitor" \
  --environment "Production Environment"

# ===== DOCUMENTATION GENERATION =====

# Publish collection documentation
postman api create \
  --name "User API Documentation" \
  --collection "User API Tests" \
  --environment "Documentation Environment"

# Update published documentation
postman api update \
  --api "User API Documentation" \
  --collection "User API Tests"

# ===== WORKSPACE COLLABORATION =====

# Create workspace for team collaboration
postman workspace create \
  --name "API Testing Team" \
  --type "team" \
  --description "Workspace for API testing collaboration"

# Add collection to workspace
postman collection import \
  --workspace "API Testing Team" \
  --file "User API Tests.postman_collection.json"

# Share environment with team
postman environment import \
  --workspace "API Testing Team" \
  --file "Shared Environment.postman_environment.json"

# ===== API TESTING WORKFLOW =====

# Complete testing workflow example

# 1. Development testing with mock server
echo "Step 1: Development testing with mock server"
postman mock create --collection "dev-collection" --name "Dev Mock"

# 2. Integration testing with staging environment
echo "Step 2: Integration testing"
newman run "integration-tests.json" -e "staging-environment.json"

# 3. Performance testing
echo "Step 3: Performance testing"
newman run "load-tests.json" -n 100 --delay-request 100

# 4. Production monitoring
echo "Step 4: Production monitoring"
postman monitor run --monitor "prod-monitor"

# 5. Documentation update
echo "Step 5: Documentation update"
postman api update --api "public-docs" --collection "latest-collection"

content.title: Mobile Application Testing Fundamentals
content.explanation: Mobile application testing requires specialized approaches that account for device diversity, touch interactions, varying screen sizes, and platform-specific behaviors. Unlike web applications, mobile apps must be tested on physical devices to accurately assess performance, touch responsiveness, sensor integration, and real-world usage scenarios. Manual testing is crucial for evaluating user experience, accessibility, and platform compliance that automated tests often miss. A comprehensive mobile testing strategy combines device testing, emulator/simulator validation, and real-world scenario assessment.

adb shell "find /data/data/com.example.app -type f -perm -o+r -o -perm -o+w"

# 4. Check logs for sensitive information
adb logcat | grep -i "password\|token\|key\|secret"

# 5. Test backup allowance
adb backup -apk -shared com.example.app

# 6. Check network traffic (requires proxy setup)
echo "Configure Burp Suite proxy and run:"
echo "adb shell settings put global http_proxy 192.168.1.100:8080"

# 7. Check for debug mode enabled
adb shell getprop ro.debuggable
adb shell getprop ro.secure

# 8. Test for hardcoded secrets in APK
strings app.apk | grep -i "api_key\|secret\|password"

# 9. Check certificate pinning
# Using objection to bypass SSL pinning
objection -g com.example.app explore \
  --startup-command "android sslpinning disable"

# 10. Test root detection bypass
objection -g com.example.app explore \
  --startup-command "android root disable"

# IOS SECURITY TESTS

# 1. Check file system permissions
# On jailbroken device:
ls -la /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/

# 2. Check Keychain entries
# Using objection:
objection -g com.example.app explore \
  --startup-command "ios keychain dump"

# 3. Check plist files for sensitive data
find /var/mobile/Containers/ -name "*.plist" -exec plutil -p {} \;

# 4. Test TouchID/FaceID bypass
objection -g com.example.app explore \
  --startup-command "ios biometrics bypass"

# 5. Check for debug symbols
nm app.ipa | grep -i "debug"

# COMMON SECURITY CHECKS

# Check for plaintext network traffic
tcpdump -i any -s 0 -w capture.pcap
# Analyze with Wireshark for HTTP traffic

# Test for insecure data storage
# Using Mobile Security Framework (MobSF)
python3 manage.py runserver  # Run MobSF
# Upload APK/IPA for automated analysis

# Test for clipboard exposure
# Monitor clipboard in app
adb shell "am broadcast -a clipper.get"

# Check for screenshot prevention
# Attempt to screenshot sensitive screens

# Test background snapshot obscuring
# Put app in background, check recent apps preview

# SECURITY TESTING AUTOMATION

# Using Frida for runtime instrumentation
frida -U -f com.example.app -l security_checks.js

# security_checks.js example:
"""
// Check for SSL pinning
Interceptor.attach(Module.findExportByName(null, "SSL_CTX_set_cert_verify_callback"), {
    onEnter: function(args) {
        console.log("SSL verification callback set");
    }
});

// Monitor cryptographic operations
var crypto = Module.findExportByName(null, "CCCrypt");
Interceptor.attach(crypto, {
    onEnter: function(args) {
        console.log("Crypto operation: " + args[0]);
    }
});
"""

# Report generation
echo "Generating security test report..."
echo "=== SECURITY TEST RESULTS ===" > security_report.txt
echo "Date: $(date)" >> security_report.txt
echo "App: com.example.app" >> security_report.txt
echo "Version: 1.0.0" >> security_report.txt
echo "" >> security_report.txt

# Add findings
echo "FINDINGS:" >> security_report.txt
echo "1. [HIGH] Plaintext credentials in SharedPreferences" >> security_report.txt
echo "2. [MEDIUM] No certificate pinning implemented" >> security_report.txt
echo "3. [LOW] Debug logging enabled in production" >> security_report.txt

echo "Security testing complete. Report saved to security_report.txt"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Generate test device matrix for iOS and Android fragmentation testing
"""

import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import List, Dict

@dataclass
class TestDevice:
    platform: str
    name: str
    model: str
    os_version: str
    screen_size: str
    screen_density: str
    chipset: str
    ram: str
    priority: str  # high, medium, low
    notes: str

class DeviceMatrixGenerator:
    """Generate comprehensive device testing matrix"""
    
    def __init__(self):
        self.ios_devices = self._get_ios_devices()
        self.android_devices = self._get_android_devices()
    
    def _get_ios_devices(self) -> List[TestDevice]:
        """iOS devices have limited fragmentation but multiple OS versions"""
        return [
            # High priority - Latest devices
            TestDevice(
                platform="iOS",
                name="iPhone 15 Pro",
                model="iPhone16,1",
                os_version="17.0",
                screen_size="6.1\"",
                screen_density="460 ppi",
                chipset="A17 Pro",
                ram="8GB",
                priority="high",
                notes="Dynamic Island, ProMotion 120Hz"
            ),
            TestDevice(
                platform="iOS",
                name="iPhone SE (3rd gen)",
                model="iPhone14,6",
                os_version="17.0",
                screen_size="4.7\"",
                screen_density="326 ppi",
                chipset="A15 Bionic",
                ram="4GB",
                priority="high",
                notes="Small screen, Touch ID"
            ),
            # Medium priority - Previous generation
            TestDevice(
                platform="iOS",
                name="iPhone 14",
                model="iPhone14,7",
                os_version="16.0",
                screen_size="6.1\"",
                screen_density="460 ppi",
                chipset="A15 Bionic",
                ram="6GB",
                priority="medium",
                notes="Notch design, one OS version behind"
            ),
            # iPad if applicable
            TestDevice(
                platform="iOS",
                name="iPad Air (5th gen)",
                model="iPad13,17",
                os_version="17.0",
                screen_size="10.9\"",
                screen_density="264 ppi",
                chipset="M1",
                ram="8GB",
                priority="medium",
                notes="Tablet form factor, Stage Manager"
            )
        ]
    
    def _get_android_devices(self) -> List[TestDevice]:
        """Android devices have extensive fragmentation"""
        return [
            # High priority - Google reference devices
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Google Pixel 8 Pro",
                model="Pixel 8 Pro",
                os_version="14",
                screen_size="6.7\"",
                screen_density="489 ppi",
                chipset="Tensor G3",
                ram="12GB",
                priority="high",
                notes="Stock Android, latest features"
            ),
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Google Pixel 7a",
                model="Pixel 7a",
                os_version="13",
                screen_size="6.1\"",
                screen_density="429 ppi",
                chipset="Tensor G2",
                ram="8GB",
                priority="high",
                notes="Mid-range reference device"
            ),
            # Samsung devices (largest market share)
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Samsung Galaxy S23 Ultra",
                model="SM-S918B",
                os_version="13",
                screen_size="6.8\"",
                screen_density="500 ppi",
                chipset="Snapdragon 8 Gen 2",
                ram="12GB",
                priority="high",
                notes="One UI, S Pen, high-end Samsung"
            ),
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Samsung Galaxy A54",
                model="SM-A546B",
                os_version="13",
                screen_size="6.4\"",
                screen_density="403 ppi",
                chipset="Exynos 1380",
                ram="8GB",
                priority="medium",
                notes="Mid-range Samsung, popular globally"
            ),
            # Xiaomi/Redmi (popular in Asia)
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Xiaomi Redmi Note 12 Pro",
                model="23021RAAEG",
                os_version="13",
                screen_size="6.67\"",
                screen_density="395 ppi",
                chipset="MediaTek Dimensity 1080",
                ram="8GB",
                priority="medium",
                notes="MIUI, popular budget device"
            ),
            # Foldable devices
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Samsung Galaxy Z Fold5",
                model="SM-F946B",
                os_version="13",
                screen_size="7.6\" (unfolded)",
                screen_density="374 ppi",
                chipset="Snapdragon 8 Gen 2",
                ram="12GB",
                priority="low",
                notes="Foldable, multi-window, hinge awareness"
            ),
            # Low-end devices
            TestDevice(
                platform="Android",
                name="Samsung Galaxy A12",
                model="SM-A125F",
                os_version="11",
                screen_size="6.5\"",
                screen_density="264 ppi",
                chipset="MediaTek Helio P35",
                ram="4GB",
                priority="low",
                notes="Low-end, limited resources"
            )
        ]
    
    def generate_test_matrix(self) -> Dict:
        """Generate comprehensive testing matrix"""
        matrix = {
            "ios": {
                "summary": {
                    "total_devices": len(self.ios_devices),
                    "os_versions": list(set(d.os_version for d in self.ios_devices)),
                    "screen_sizes": list(set(d.screen_size for d in self.ios_devices)),
                    "testing_focus": "OS versions, screen sizes, feature support"
                },
                "devices": [self._device_to_dict(d) for d in self.ios_devices]
            },
            "android": {
                "summary": {
                    "total_devices": len(self.android_devices),
                    "manufacturers": list(set(d.name.split()[0] for d in self.android_devices)),
                    "os_versions": list(set(d.os_version for d in self.android_devices)),
                    "screen_sizes": list(set(d.screen_size for d in self.android_devices)),
                    "testing_focus": "Fragmentation, manufacturer customizations, performance variations"
                },
                "devices": [self._device_to_dict(d) for d in self.android_devices]
            },
            "testing_recommendations": {
                "ios": [
                    "Focus on latest 2-3 iOS versions",
                    "Test on different screen sizes (small, standard, large)",
                    "Verify Dynamic Island compatibility if applicable",
                    "Test with different accessibility settings"
                ],
                "android": [
                    "Test on minimum 3 different manufacturers",
                    "Include devices with different screen densities",
                    "Test with different Android versions (11, 12, 13, 14)",
                    "Verify compatibility with manufacturer skins (One UI, MIUI, etc.)",
                    "Test on low-end devices for performance issues"
                ]
            }
        }
        
        return matrix
    
    def _device_to_dict(self, device: TestDevice) -> Dict:
        """Convert TestDevice to dictionary"""
        return {
            "name": device.name,
            "model": device.model,
            "os_version": device.os_version,
            "screen_size": device.screen_size,
            "screen_density": device.screen_density,
            "chipset": device.chipset,
            "ram": device.ram,
            "priority": device.priority,
            "notes": device.notes
        }
    
    def generate_test_plan(self, matrix: Dict) -> str:
        """Generate human-readable test plan"""
        plan = "# Cross-Platform Device Testing Plan\n\n"
        
        plan += "## iOS Testing Strategy\n"
        plan += f"Total devices to test: {matrix['ios']['summary']['total_devices']}\n"
        plan += f"OS versions: {', '.join(matrix['ios']['summary']['os_versions'])}\n\n"
        
        plan += "### High Priority Devices\n"
        for device in matrix['ios']['devices']:
            if device['priority'] == 'high':
                plan += f"- **{device['name']}** ({device['os_version']}): {device['notes']}\n"
        
        plan += "\n## Android Testing Strategy\n"
        plan += f"Total devices to test: {matrix['android']['summary']['total_devices']}\n"
        plan += f"Manufacturers: {', '.join(matrix['android']['summary']['manufacturers'])}\n"
        plan += f"OS versions: {', '.join(matrix['android']['summary']['os_versions'])}\n\n"
        
        plan += "### Testing Priority Distribution\n"
        priorities = {'high': 0, 'medium': 0, 'low': 0}
        for device in matrix['android']['devices']:
            priorities[device['priority']] += 1
        
        plan += f"- High priority: {priorities['high']} devices (critical for launch)\n"
        plan += f"- Medium priority: {priorities['medium']} devices (important for coverage)\n"
        plan += f"- Low priority: {priorities['low']} devices (nice to have)\n"
        
        return plan

if __name__ == "__main__":
    generator = DeviceMatrixGenerator()
    matrix = generator.generate_test_matrix()
    
    # Save as JSON
    with open("device_test_matrix.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(matrix, f, indent=2)
    
    # Generate and save test plan
    test_plan = generator.generate_test_plan(matrix)
    with open("test_plan.md", "w") as f:
        f.write(test_plan)
    
    print(f"Generated device matrix with {len(generator.ios_devices)} iOS devices")
    print(f"and {len(generator.android_devices)} Android devices")
    print("Files saved: device_test_matrix.json, test_plan.md")
